federal_baseline: You have a First Amendment right to photograph and record police officers performing their official duties in public. Nine federal appeals courts — the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 7th, 9th, 10th, and 11th Circuits — have recognized this right, most recently the 2nd Circuit in 2026 (Massimino v. Benoit). The U.S. Supreme Court has never ruled on it directly, so the exact boundaries can still vary by place. The right does not protect interfering with officers, trespassing to get the shot, or breaking other valid laws while recording.

Alabama.notes: You can record a conversation you are part of without telling anyone. On-duty police in public have no expectation of privacy, and the 11th Circuit (Smith v. City of Cumming, 2000) protects filming them.

Alaska.notes: A 2025 governor-backed bill (SB 85) would have switched Alaska to all-party consent, but it stalled in committee and never passed. The 9th Circuit (Fordyce v. City of Seattle) protects filming police doing their jobs in public.

Arizona.buffer_zone: 8-foot buffer law (HB 2319) struck down permanently — not in effect
Arizona.notes: The 2022 law that made it a misdemeanor to film police within 8 feet was permanently blocked by a federal judge in July 2023 as unconstitutional; the state declined to defend it. The 9th Circuit's Fordyce v. City of Seattle also protects filming police in public.

Arkansas.notes: Recording a conversation you are part of is legal with just your own consent. No Arkansas-specific court ruling on filming police was verified; a 2015 right-to-record bill (HB 1669) was proposed but its passage could not be verified.

California.notes: Section 632 only covers 'confidential' conversations, and on-duty police in public have no expectation of privacy, so recording them is not eavesdropping. Since 2015, Cal. Penal Code § 148(g) says filming a public officer in public is not obstruction and does not justify a stop or arrest.

Colorado.notes: Colorado goes further than most states: a 2015 law (now C.R.S. § 16-3-311) explicitly gives people the right to record police incidents, and officers who seize or destroy a recording face damages plus a $15,000 civil penalty under C.R.S. § 13-21-128.

Connecticut.consent_citation: Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 53a-187, 53a-189 (criminal); Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-570d (civil, phone calls)
Connecticut.notes: Criminally it is one-party, but phone calls are all-party by civil law (§ 52-570d), so do not secretly record phone calls. In August 2026 the 2nd Circuit (Massimino v. Waterbury) recognized a First Amendment right to film police in public — binding in Connecticut.

Delaware.notes: Delaware has two recording statutes that appear to conflict (§ 2402(c)(4) reads one-party; § 1335(a)(4) requires all-party consent), and no court has resolved it — treat it as all-party to be safe. Either way, the 3rd Circuit (Fields v. City of Philadelphia, 2017) protects filming police in public.

Florida.buffer_zone: 25-foot HALO law (Fla. SB 184, 2024) — in effect since Jan. 1, 2025
Florida.notes: Section 934.03 only protects conversations with a real expectation of privacy, which on-duty officers in public do not have — the 11th Circuit (Smith v. City of Cumming, 2000) protects filming them. Under the HALO law, after a verbal warning you must stay 25 feet back from a first responder on duty, but the law itself says peaceful audio/video recording is a legitimate purpose and not harassment by itself.

Georgia.notes: Audio recording needs only one party's consent; video of people in private places out of public view needs everyone's consent (§ 16-11-62(2)) — filming police in public is fine. Smith v. City of Cumming (11th Cir. 2000), a Georgia case, is the landmark federal ruling protecting filming police.

Hawaii.notes: Hawaii's eavesdropping law is one-party consent. The privacy statute (Haw. Rev. Stat. § 711-1111(1)(d)) expressly permits recording officers performing their duties when they have no reasonable expectation of privacy. The Hawaii Supreme Court held in State v. Russo (407 P.3d 137, 2017) that filming on-duty police in public is protected by the First Amendment and the state constitution.

Idaho.notes: Idaho is a one-party consent state; a participant may record without telling others, but recording a conversation you are not part of is barred. No Idaho-specific court ruling on recording police was found, and no state buffer-zone law was found. The First Amendment right recognized by federal courts applies.

Illinois.notes: Illinois was all-party, but the old eavesdropping law was struck down in People v. Melongo and People v. Clark (Ill. 2014) and, as applied to recording police, by ACLU v. Alvarez (7th Cir. 2012). The replacement law covers only private conversations where parties have a reasonable expectation of privacy, which does not include on-duty officers in public.

Indiana.buffer_zone: 25-foot law (Ind. Code § 35-44.1-2-14, HEA 1186) — BLOCKED, not in effect
Indiana.notes: Indiana is one-party consent. Its 2023 25-foot buffer-zone law was preliminarily enjoined in Sept. 2024 and the Seventh Circuit upheld the block in Aug. 2025 (Reporters Comm. v. Rokita), finding it unconstitutionally vague. The 7th Circuit (Alvarez) also protects recording police as First Amendment activity.

Iowa.notes: Iowa is a one-party consent state; a participant may record a communication they are part of. No Iowa-specific court ruling on recording police was found, and no state buffer-zone law was found. The ACLU of Iowa confirms filming in public spaces is generally protected.

Kansas.buffer_zone: 25-foot 'Halo Act' buffer law (HB 2372) — enacted April 2026 via veto override; enforcement/challenge status unverified
Kansas.notes: Kansas is one-party consent; the state supreme court confirmed it in State v. Roudybush (686 P.2d 100, 1984). The Tenth Circuit (Irizarry v. Yehia, 2022) held there is a clearly established First Amendment right to record police in public. The 25-foot buffer law for first responders is very new and press groups called it likely unconstitutional; no court ruling on it was found.

Kentucky.notes: Kentucky is one-party consent: 'eavesdrop' is defined as recording without the consent of at least one party. No Kentucky-specific court ruling on recording police and no state buffer-zone law were found.

Louisiana.buffer_zone: 25-foot law (La. R.S. § 14:108.1.1) — BLOCKED, not in effect
Louisiana.notes: Louisiana is one-party consent. The 2024 25-foot buffer law took effect Aug. 1, 2024, but a federal judge (M.D. La., Jan. 31, 2025) preliminarily enjoined enforcement as unconstitutionally vague; the state's appeal was pending in the Fifth Circuit as of 2026. The Fifth Circuit held in Turner v. Driver (2017) that a First Amendment right to record police exists.

Maine.notes: Maine is one-party consent for wire and oral communications under its interception statute. No Maine-specific court ruling on recording police and no state buffer-zone law were found; federal courts protect recording on-duty officers in public.

Maryland.consent_citation: Md. Code Ann., Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 10-402
Maryland.notes: Maryland is all-party consent; recording audio without every party's consent is a felony. But case law holds the wiretap law does not cover on-duty officers in public: in Maryland v. Graber (Harford Co. Cir. Ct. 2010), felony wiretap charges against a motorcyclist who recorded a trooper at a traffic stop were dismissed because the officer had no reasonable expectation of privacy.

Massachusetts.notes: Secret audio recording of anyone (including police) is a crime, but merely making the recording obvious — e.g., holding a phone up — satisfies the law since only actual knowledge, not formal consent, is required. Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir. 2011), held openly filming police in public is protected by the First Amendment. Secretly recording officers during a traffic stop was upheld as a crime in Commonwealth v. Hyde, 434 Mass. 594 (2001).

Michigan.notes: Michigan's eavesdropping statute is written broadly, but courts have long applied a 'participant exception' — if you are a party to the conversation you may record it (Sullivan v. Gray, 117 Mich. App. 476 (1982)). Filming on-duty police in public is treated as First Amendment-protected; no Michigan law specifically restricts recording officers.

Minnesota.notes: One-party consent state: any participant may record a conversation. Minneapolis's January 2025 DOJ consent decree explicitly orders officers not to interfere with civilians photographing or recording them in public. Some federal sources note the First Amendment right to record police is not yet 'clearly established' in the 8th Circuit, which affects civil suits against officers.

Mississippi.notes: One-party consent state: a person who is a party to a communication (or has one party's consent) may lawfully record it. No Mississippi law restricts filming on-duty police in public; Turner v. Driver, 848 F.3d 678 (5th Cir. 2017), protects recording police as First Amendment activity.

Missouri.notes: One-party consent state: only one party to a conversation must consent. A 2023 bill (HB 1081) that would have made Missouri an all-party consent state did not pass. No Missouri law sets a distance buffer for recording police.

Montana.notes: Montana bars recording a conversation with a hidden device 'without the knowledge of all parties' — so notifying everyone you are recording (not their approval) satisfies the law. Openly filming officers on duty is protected by the First Amendment in the 9th Circuit (Fordyce v. City of Seattle). No Montana buffer-zone law exists.

Nebraska.notes: One-party consent state: a party to a conversation may record it without telling the others. A 2024 bill (LB1185) that would have required recorders to stay 10 feet from officers was 'indefinitely postponed' and never became law, so no buffer zone exists.

Nevada.notes: Nevada is split: face-to-face conversations need only one party's consent (NRS 200.650), while phone calls need all-party consent (NRS 200.620). Nevada goes further than most states to protect filming: NRS 171.1233, enacted 2020, expressly says anyone may record law enforcement activity and bars officers from preventing, threatening, or ordering someone to stop recording.

New Hampshire.notes: All-party consent state for private conversations, but Gericke v. Begin, 753 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2014), held that openly filming police during a traffic stop in New Hampshire is a clearly established First Amendment right. RSA 91-A separately gives an explicit right to record public meetings. No buffer-zone law exists.

New Jersey.notes: One-party consent state: any participant may record a conversation without the others knowing. Fields v. City of Philadelphia, 862 F.3d 353 (3d Cir. 2017), which covers New Jersey, recognizes a First Amendment right to record police performing their duties in public. No buffer-zone law exists.

New Mexico.notes: The 10th Circuit (Irizarry v. Yehia, 2022), which covers New Mexico, held the First Amendment protects filming on-duty police in public and that the right was clearly established by 2019. Simply recording from a safe distance is not obstructing an officer (N.M. Stat. Ann. § 30-22-1), but physically interfering still can be.

New York.notes: New York's Right to Record Act (Civil Rights Law § 79-p, 2020) lets people sue if officials interfere with recording police activity. The 2nd Circuit (Massimino v. Benoit, 2026) recognized a clearly established First Amendment right to record police in public going forward. The NY Court of Appeals (Reyes, 2026) held there is no right to film inside police station lobbies, and an NYPD policy banning it stands.

North Carolina.notes: The 4th Circuit (Sharpe v. Winterville Police Department, 2023), which covers North Carolina, held that recording and livestreaming your own traffic stop is protected speech. Filming itself is not obstructing an officer (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 14-223), but an officer can still enforce orders aimed at genuine interference.

North Dakota.notes: The 8th Circuit has not squarely recognized a First Amendment right to record police (see Akins v. Knight, 2017; Molina v. City of St. Louis, 2023), though federal district courts in the circuit have upheld it. Chestnut v. Wallace (8th Cir. 2020) protects watching police-citizen interactions from a distance without interfering.

Ohio.buffer_zone: 15-foot law (H.B. 20, signed July 7, 2026) — in effect since Oct. 6, 2026
Ohio.notes: People may not approach or remain within 15 feet of a first responder after a verbal warning, but only when they also interfere with the responder's duties or threaten physical harm — simply observing or recording is not prohibited on its own. The 6th Circuit has no binding decision, but federal district courts in Ohio treat the right to openly film police as clearly established (Higginbotham v. City of Cleveland, N.D. Ohio 2015).

Oklahoma.notes: The 10th Circuit (Irizarry v. Yehia, 2022), which covers Oklahoma, held the First Amendment protects filming on-duty police in public and that the right was clearly established by 2019. Recording itself is not obstructing an officer (Okla. Stat. tit. 21, § 540), but physically getting in the way still is.

Oregon.consent: hybrid (one-party for phone/radio calls; all participants must be informed for in-person conversations)
Oregon.notes: Oregon law expressly allows recording an on-duty officer performing official duties, openly and where you may lawfully be (ORS 165.540(5)(b)); the all-parties-must-be-informed rule for other conversations was upheld by the 9th Circuit en banc in Project Veritas v. Schmidt (2025). The 9th Circuit recognized a right to film police in public in Fordyce v. City of Seattle (1995).

Pennsylvania.notes: Courts have narrowed the wiretap law for police recording: officers performing duties in public have no reasonable expectation of privacy, so recording them is not a wiretap violation (Kelly v. Borough of Carlisle, 3d Cir. 2010). The 3rd Circuit (Fields v. City of Philadelphia, 2017) recognized a First Amendment right to record on-duty police in public.

Rhode Island.notes: The 1st Circuit (Glik v. Cunniffe, 2011), which covers Rhode Island, held there is a clearly established right to openly record on-duty police in public; Gericke v. Begin (1st Cir. 2014) extended it to traffic stops. The right does not protect physically interfering with officers, only recording.

South Carolina.notes: The 4th Circuit (Sharpe v. Winterville Police Department, 2023), which covers South Carolina, held that recording and livestreaming your own traffic stop is protected speech, and the right is now clearly established in the circuit. Interfering with officers (S.C. Code Ann. § 16-9-340) is still punishable — the protection covers recording, not getting in the way.

South Dakota.notes: South Dakota is one-party consent: the law only bans recording by someone 'not present during' the conversation without a party's consent, so a participant may record. No South Dakota buffer-zone law was found. The 8th Circuit has not squarely recognized a First Amendment right to record police, though federal district courts in the circuit have upheld it.

Tennessee.buffer_zone: 25-foot 'PEACE Act' (Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-16-611, SB30/HB55) — in effect since July 1, 2025; statute number per ACLU of Tennessee explainer
Tennessee.notes: After an officer orders you to stop or retreat, knowingly approaching or staying within 25 feet while the officer performs official duties is a Class B misdemeanor, with an affirmative defense if the warning was not received or understood. No binding 6th Circuit ruling recognizes a right to record police in public. The 25-foot law is being challenged in two federal lawsuits (a media-coalition suit and an ACLU suit); both were pending as of fall 2026.

Texas.buffer_zone: none in effect (a 2015 proposal, HB 2918, to criminalize filming police within 25 feet was dropped and never enacted)
Texas.notes: Turner v. Driver, 848 F.3d 678 (5th Cir. 2017): the First Amendment protects recording police in public, subject to reasonable time, place, and manner limits. Officers can still order bystanders back for safety under the interference-with-public-duties law (Tex. Penal Code § 38.15).

Utah.notes: Utah law says recording an officer performing official duties in plain view is not, by itself, interference with a peace officer (Utah Code § 76-8-305(4)). Irizarry v. Yehia, 38 F.4th 1282 (10th Cir. 2022), held the First Amendment right to film police in public is clearly established.

Vermont.buffer_zone: none in effect (a 25-foot first-responder buffer bill, H.697, was debated in early 2026 but held for further drafting, not enacted)
Vermont.consent_citation: No state statute; one-party rule applies by default under federal law, 18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d)
Vermont.notes: The Vermont Supreme Court in State v. Geraw (2002) barred secret recording where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy (e.g., inside a home), but on-duty police in public have no such expectation. The Vermont League of Cities and Towns advises that recording may take place in any public space, including police station lobbies.

Virginia.notes: Sharpe v. Winterville Police Dept., 59 F.4th 674 (4th Cir. 2023), held that livestreaming a police traffic stop is protected speech, though it did not decide a general right to record. Consent is not needed at all to record conversations in public where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy.

Washington.notes: State v. Flora (Wash. Ct. App. 1992) held that conversations with police during an arrest are not 'private,' so the all-party-consent law does not bar recording on-duty police in public. The state attorney general has also opined that interactions with on-duty police are presumed public. The 9th Circuit recognized a First Amendment right to film matters of public interest in Fordyce v. City of Seattle (1995).

West Virginia.buffer_zone: 30-foot law (W. Va. Code § 61-5-30, Enr. Comm. Sub. for SB 4) — in effect since June 12, 2026; no court ruling on it yet found
West Virginia.notes: After a verbal warning, knowingly and willfully approaching or staying within 30 feet of a first responder while acting to impede/interfere or threaten/menace is a misdemeanor ($50-$500 fine and/or up to 1 year in jail). Sharpe v. Winterville Police Dept. (4th Cir. 2023), which covers West Virginia, held livestreaming a police traffic stop is protected speech.

Wisconsin.notes: ACLU v. Alvarez, 679 F.3d 583 (7th Cir. 2012), held the First Amendment protects openly recording police performing duties in public. In August 2025 the 7th Circuit (which covers Wisconsin) struck down Indiana's 25-foot police buffer law as unconstitutionally vague.

Wyoming.notes: No consent is needed to record conversations in public where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy. Irizarry v. Yehia, 38 F.4th 1282 (10th Cir. 2022), which covers Wyoming, held the First Amendment right to film police in public is clearly established.
